passage: Monday. Devika refused the green bottle at water time. "Kiran and Mihir and Tara have blue ones," she said, clutching her blue lid. Tara shrugged and went on drinking. Thursday. The four of them played shop. Devika said the rule was that everyone must be the shopkeeper, and Mihir agreed at once; Kiran frowned but said nothing. Next Tuesday. The teacher gave out red and yellow ribbons for the dance. Devika looked at Kiran's, took the same colour, and danced the same step a beat behind him, smiling only when he smiled back.

qa.q: Why did Devika clutch the blue lid on Monday?
qa.a: Devika clutched the blue lid because Kiran, Mihir and Tara have blue ones.

qa.q: What might Devika feel when her ribbon matches Kiran's and Kiran smiles back?
qa.a: Devika seems to feel safe and included; smiling only when Kiran smiles suggests sameness reassures Devika.

qa.q: What small step could the teacher take to help Devika feel safe while trying something different?
qa.a: The teacher could let Devika keep one thing the same as the group and try one small difference beside another child, so being different is not lonely.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel about Devika's shop rule that everyone must be the shopkeeper?
qa.a: Kiran frowns but says nothing, which suggests Kiran is unhappy with the rule but would rather keep the game going than argue.

grounding: A child wants the same bottle, game rule and dance step as the group because sameness feels safe, shown across three days.

passage: Rain drummed on the roof, so the sports-day dance was squeezed into the tiny library with ten minutes left before the buses. The teacher showed a new step: two claps and a jump. Kunal did it at once, then Ravi and Sana. Yogesh stood still, watching their feet. "Everybody is doing the same one," he whispered, and copied them, one beat late. Only Hema kept her old arm wave. Yogesh glanced at her, edged closer to Kunal, and did not look at Hema again until the bell rang.

qa.q: Why was the sports-day dance practised in the tiny library?
qa.a: Rain drummed on the roof, so the sports-day dance was squeezed into the tiny library.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh copy the new step one beat late?
qa.a: Yogesh saw everybody doing the same step and whispered that they were all doing the same one, so copying felt safer than standing out; the feeling is a wish to belong.

qa.q: What could the teacher say to Yogesh that keeps both belonging and difference possible?
qa.a: The teacher could say that a group can share one dance and still let a person add a small touch, so being different is not the same as being left out.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hema to keep her arm wave while the others do the new step?
qa.a: Hema may feel a little alone yet sure of her own step; Hema keeps going even when Yogesh glances over and edges away.

grounding: A child insists on the same dance step as the group, and time pressure in a cramped room makes sameness feel safer than difference.
